blocks.html: Look around you. Some things are living, like a dog, a tree or you. Some things are not living, like a rock or a toy car. How can we tell?
A living thing grows, needs food and water, and makes new living things like itself.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A tree grows and needs water, even though it stays in one place.
A toy car moves, but it does not grow, eat or drink.
A cloud moves, but it does not grow from food or make baby clouds.

opts.readme: Your child taps a card, then a group. Talk about the tree and the car.

blocks.cap: Sort the pictures: living or not living?

blocks.html: Moving is not the test. A toy car moves, but it never grows. A tree stays still, but it grows taller every year and drinks water through its roots.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Is a cat living?
steps: Does a cat grow? Yes, a kitten grows into a cat.
Does a cat need food and water? Yes.
Can cats have kittens? Yes.
blocks.a: Yes, a cat is living.

blocks.html: Some children say a car, a cloud or a fire is alive because it moves, and that a tree is not alive because it stays still. Ask the three questions instead: Does it grow? Does it need food and water? Does it make new ones like itself?
For the grown-up. A seed is alive too: it is resting until it gets water. You can sprout a bean on a damp paper towel to see it wake up.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 1.1 Themes and Concepts of Biology (properties of life)

blocks.html: You need water, food and air every day. So do all animals. Plants need some of the same things, but they are different in one big way.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: What living things need.

blocks.html: All living things need water. Animals need food and air. Plants need light, water and air, and they make their own food.
Animals cannot make food, so they must eat plants or other animals. Plants catch sunlight with their green leaves and use it to make food from air and water.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Does a rabbit need to eat?
steps: A rabbit is an animal.
Animals cannot make their own food.
A rabbit eats grass and other plants.
blocks.a: Yes. A rabbit needs food, water and air.

blocks.html: Many children think plants eat soil, or that we must feed them like pets. Plants need water and light from us, and they make their own food in their leaves.
For the grown-up. Living things also need space to live and grow. A crowded fish bowl or a pot packed with seedlings is a good example to talk about.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes
Next Generation Science Standards, K-ESS3-1: Earth and Human Activity

blocks.html: A log is not growing. A seashell does not eat. Are they living? Not anymore! They came from something that was living.
Living things grow now. Once-living things came from a plant or an animal. Never-living things, like rocks and coins, never grew at all.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A log is wood from a tree.
A sea animal grew this shell.
It grew on a tree, then fell.

opts.readme: Your child taps a card, then a group. Ask: where did it come from?

blocks.cap: Three groups: living, once living and never living.

blocks.html: Ask where it came from. Wood comes from trees. Paper is made from wood. A feather grew on a bird. Those were all part of living things once.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Is a wooden chair living, once living or never living?
steps: A chair does not grow, so it is not living now.
It is made of wood.
Wood came from a tree, which was alive.
blocks.a: Once living.

blocks.html: Children often call a dry leaf or a log "never living" because it does not grow. Ask: did it come from a plant or an animal? If yes, it is once living.

For the grown-up. Go on a short walk and collect a few things: a leaf, a twig, a pebble, a feather someone dropped. Sort them at home into living, once living and never living, and ask "Where did it come from?" for each one.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS2-1: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (decomposers return once-living matter to the soil)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 1.1 Themes and Concepts of Biology (properties of life)

blocks.html: You were once a tiny baby. Now you are bigger! All living things start small and grow. Some change shape as they grow, too.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Young and grown-up: a tadpole becomes a frog, a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, a sprout becomes a tree.

blocks.html: Living things grow from small to big, and many change how they look as they grow.
A young living thing grows into a grown-up of its own kind. A tadpole looks like a little fish, but it is a young frog. It can only grow into a frog.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: What does a caterpillar grow into?
steps: A caterpillar eats leaves and grows.
It makes a chrysalis.
It comes out as a butterfly.
blocks.a: A butterfly.

blocks.html: Children think young living things are just smaller copies of their parents. Many are, like kittens and chicks. But a tadpole and a caterpillar look very different from the grown-ups they become.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Your child taps two pictures to swap them, then presses Check.

blocks.cap: Put the frog's life in order.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Baby pictures help here. Put a photo of your child as a baby next to one from today, and talk about what changed and what stayed the same.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 1-LS3-1: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits
Next Generation Science Standards, 3-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (life cycles)

blocks.html: A plant cannot walk to a sunny spot or get itself a drink. It needs us, or the rain and the sun, to give it what it needs.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Point to each arrow: light, water, and air going in.

blocks.cap: Light, water and air go into a plant.

blocks.html: Plants need light, water, air, nutrients from the soil, and room to grow.

The leaves use light, air and water to make the plant's food. The roots drink water from the soil and take in a little of the nutrients there. Without light or water, the plant cannot make food, so it droops and turns pale.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Two bean plants start the same. One is by a sunny window. One is in a dark closet. Which grows better?
steps: Plants need light to make food.
The plant by the window gets light.
The plant in the closet gets none.
blocks.a: The plant by the sunny window.

blocks.html: Many children (and grown-ups!) think plants get their food from the soil. The soil gives water and a few nutrients. The food itself is made in the green leaves.
For the grown-up. Try it together: Plant two bean seeds in cups. Put one in a sunny window and one in a dark cupboard after they sprout. Look every day and talk about what you see.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS2-1: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (plants need sunlight and water)
Next Generation Science Standards, K-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 5.1 Overview of Photosynthesis

blocks.html: A plant has parts, just like you have arms and legs. Each part has a job.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Tap each part together and read its job.

blocks.cap: Tap a part to see its job.

blocks.html: Most plants have roots, a stem, leaves and flowers.

items: Roots hold the plant in the ground and drink water.
The stem holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves.

blocks.html: Each part helps the plant get what it needs. Roots reach down for water, and the stem lifts the leaves up toward the light.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Ask your child to tap the stem.

blocks.cap: Find the stem.

blocks.html: Children forget the roots because they are hidden under the ground. Some think a tree is not a plant because it is big and woody. A tree has roots, a stem (its trunk), leaves and flowers too.
For the grown-up. Pull up a weed (or look at a carrot with its green top) and find the roots, the stem and the leaves together. Talk about the job of each part as you go.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (structures and functions)

blocks.html: Pull up a weed and look at the bottom. You will see thin, twisty strings. Those are roots. Most of the time they hide under the ground, so we forget about them. But a plant could not live without them.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Ask your child to tap the roots. Then talk about why they are under the ground.

blocks.cap: Find the roots.

blocks.html: Roots hold the plant in the ground and take in water and nutrients from the soil.

Water is in the soil, so the roots grow down to reach it. They spread out wide, like fingers holding on, so wind and rain cannot knock the plant over. The water they drink goes up the stem to the leaves.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Sam sprays water on a plant's leaves, but the soil stays dry. Will the plant get the water it needs?
steps: Where does most of a plant's water come in? Through its roots.
The roots are in the soil.
The soil is still dry, so the roots have nothing to drink.
blocks.a: No. Sam should water the soil, so the roots can drink.

blocks.html: Many children think roots only hold the plant up, or that a plant drinks through its leaves. Holding on is one job. Drinking is the other big job, and most of a plant's water comes in through its roots.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Both grow under the ground, but only one is a root.

blocks.cap: A carrot is a big root we can eat.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Some roots also store food for the plant, like carrots, beets and radishes. A potato grows underground too, but it is a stem, which you will meet in Plant Parts We Eat.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (structures and functions)

blocks.html: You know the roots drink water. But how does the water get all the way up to the leaves? It climbs up the stem!

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Watch the dots. Blue goes up from the roots. Gold goes down from the leaves.

blocks.cap: Water goes up the stem. Food goes down.

blocks.html: The stem holds the plant up and carries water up and food down. The leaves catch sunlight and make the plant's food.

Leaves need light to make food, so the stem lifts them up toward the sun. Inside the stem are tiny tubes, like drinking straws. Water rides up the tubes to the leaves. Food made in the leaves travels down to feed the roots.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A white flower stands in a cup of water with blue food coloring. The next day its petals have blue edges. How did the blue get there?
steps: The bottom of the stem was in the blue water.
Tiny tubes in the stem carried the water up.
The water reached the petals, and the blue color came along.
blocks.a: Up through the stem.

blocks.html: Some children think a stem is just a stick with no job. It is the plant's pipe and its pole. A tree trunk is a stem too: a big, woody one.

For the grown-up. Try the blue-flower test with a white carnation, a daisy, or a stalk of celery (celery's stalk holds up its leaves and works the same way). Use a fresh cut and a few drops of food coloring, and check the next morning.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (structures and functions)

blocks.html: Flowers are pretty, but they also have a big job. A flower is where a plant makes its seeds. Then a fruit grows around the seeds to hold them and keep them safe.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Point to the petals, then to the base of the pistil, where the seeds form.

blocks.cap: The parts of a flower. Seeds form at the base of the pistil.

blocks.html: Flowers make seeds. A fruit is the part of a plant that holds the seeds.
After a flower blooms, its petals fall off. The part in the middle swells up into a fruit with seeds inside. That is why you find seeds when you cut open an apple, a pumpkin or a tomato.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A tomato is full of seeds, so it is a fruit.
A carrot is a root.
Lettuce is leaves.
A pea pod holds the pea seeds, so it is a fruit.

opts.readme: Ask for each one: does it have seeds inside?

blocks.cap: Does it hold seeds? Then it is a fruit.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A tomato is not sweet. Is it a fruit?
steps: Cut a tomato open.
It is full of small seeds.
The part of a plant that holds seeds is a fruit.
blocks.a: Yes. A tomato is a fruit.

blocks.html: Children often call only sweet foods fruits. To a scientist, sweet does not matter. A tomato, a cucumber, a pumpkin and a pea pod are all fruits, because they hold seeds.
For the grown-up. In the kitchen we call tomatoes and cucumbers vegetables, and that is fine for cooking. In science, "fruit" means the part that holds the seeds.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS2-2: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics
OpenStax, Biology 2e, 32.1 Reproductive Development and Structure (flowers and fruit)

blocks.html: Watch a bee on a flower. It pokes its head in and drinks a sweet juice called nectar. When it flies away, it carries yellow dust on its fuzzy body. That dust is pollen.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Find the pollen on the flower and the bee.

blocks.cap: Pollen sticks to the bee.

blocks.html: Bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and the wind carry pollen from flower to flower. That helps the flowers make seeds.

Most flowers need pollen from another flower of the same kind before they can make seeds. A flower cannot walk over and get it. So animals that come for nectar carry the pollen for it, without even knowing.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A bee drinks from an apple blossom, then flies to another apple blossom. What did it bring?
steps: The bee came for nectar, its food.
Pollen from the first blossom stuck to its body.
Some of that pollen rubs off on the second blossom.
blocks.a: Pollen, which helps the second blossom make seeds.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Pollen carriers. Grass and corn use the wind.

blocks.html: Children often think bees visit flowers to help them. Bees come for their own food. Carrying pollen happens along the way, and it helps both of them.
For the grown-up. On a sunny day, sit near a flowering bush and count the visitors for two minutes. Look for pollen on their legs. Watch from a calm distance and let them work.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS2-2: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics

blocks.html: Seeds cannot walk, but many of them travel far! Some fly, some float, some hitch a ride, and some get popped out of a pod.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Its fluffy top is like a little umbrella.
Its wing spins like a helicopter.
It floats across the sea.
Its tiny hooks catch on fur.
Animals eat the fruit and drop the seeds.
The dry pod splits open.

opts.readme: Look at each shape together. How could it travel?

blocks.cap: How does each seed travel?

blocks.html: Seeds travel by wind, water, animals, or by popping out of a pod.

Under a big plant it is shady and crowded. A seed that lands far away has more room, light and water to grow. The shape of a seed is a clue to how it travels: fluff and wings for wind, hooks for fur, tasty fruit for hungry animals.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A burr sticks to a dog's fur on a walk. What happens to the seed inside?
steps: The burr has tiny hooks that grab fur.
The dog carries it along.
Later it falls off, far from its parent plant.
blocks.a: It may grow into a new plant in a new place.

blocks.html: Many children think every seed just drops to the ground under its parent. Some do, but most plants have a way to send their seeds farther, where a new plant has room.
For the grown-up. After a walk in a field, check socks and pant legs for burrs and stick-tights. Those are seeds on a ride. In fall, look for spinning maple seeds and blowing dandelion fluff.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS2-2: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics

blocks.html: A seed looks like a tiny pebble. But inside, a baby plant is curled up and waiting, with a packed lunch of food beside it. Give it water and warmth, and it wakes up!

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

notes: A seed holds a tiny plant and food for it.
It soaks up water. A root grows down, then a shoot grows up.
Leaves open and start making food from light.
Flowers become pods full of new seeds.
opts.readme: Press Next together and read each note.

blocks.cap: From seed to sprout and beyond.

blocks.html: A seed needs water, warmth and air to sprout. A root grows down first, then a shoot grows up toward the light.
Under the soil it is dark, so a young plant cannot make food yet. It uses the food stored inside the seed. When its first leaves reach the light, it can start making its own.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A bean seed is planted in dark, damp soil. Can it sprout?
steps: It has water from the damp soil.
It has food stored inside the seed.
It does not need light until its leaves come up.
blocks.a: Yes. Bean seeds sprout in the dark.

blocks.html: Many children think a seed needs sunlight to sprout. Beans, peas and corn sprout in the dark soil. The young plant needs light once its first leaves come up.

For the grown-up. Fold a damp paper towel inside a clear cup or a zip bag and tuck in two or three dry beans. Keep it damp and warm. In a few days you will see the root come out first, then the shoot.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS2-1: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (plants need water and light to grow)
OpenStax, Biology 2e, 32.2 Pollination and Fertilization (seed germination)

blocks.html: A bean plant has a life story. It starts as a seed and ends by making new seeds. Then the story starts all over again. That is why we call it a life cycle: it goes around like a circle.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Start at the seed at the top and follow the arrows around.

blocks.cap: The life cycle of a bean plant.

blocks.html: Seed → sprout → young plant → adult plant with flowers → pod (fruit) with seeds, and around again.
A plant has to grow big and strong before it can make flowers. The flowers make seeds, and a pod grows around them. When the new seeds land in soil, each one can start a new plant.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Which comes first: the young plant or the flowers?
steps: A sprout grows more leaves and becomes a young plant.
The young plant keeps growing.
When it is grown, it makes flowers.
blocks.a: The young plant comes first.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Your child taps two pictures to swap them, then presses Check.

blocks.cap: Put the bean plant's life in order.

blocks.html: Children sometimes put the flowers before the young plant, or stop at the flowers. Remember the end: the flowers turn into a pod with seeds, and the seeds start the cycle again.
For the grown-up. If you sprouted beans in A Seed Starts to Grow, plant one in a pot by a sunny window. Bush beans can flower and make pods in a couple of months.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (life cycles)

blocks.html: You eat breakfast, lunch and dinner. A plant never eats at all! Instead, it makes its own food, right inside its green leaves.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Point to each arrow: light, air and water go in; oxygen comes out; sugar is the food.

blocks.cap: What goes into a leaf, and what comes out.

blocks.html: Green leaves use sunlight, air and water to make sugar, the plant's food. They give off oxygen, the gas we breathe.

Light gives the leaf energy. The leaf uses that energy to join a gas from the air, called carbon dioxide, with water from the roots. Together they become sugar. The plant uses the sugar to live and to build new leaves, stems and wood.

blocks.title: A famous test
blocks.q: Long ago, a scientist named van Helmont grew a willow tree in a pot for five years. The tree grew from 5 pounds to 169 pounds. Did it eat the soil?
steps: He weighed the soil at the start and at the end.
The soil had lost only about 2 ounces.
The tree had gained about 164 pounds.
blocks.a: No. The tree was not built from soil. We know now it was built mostly from air and water.

blocks.html: Many people think a plant eats soil, so a big tree must have used up lots of dirt. The soil gives water and a few nutrients. The tree itself is built mostly from air and water, put together with the energy of sunlight.

For the grown-up. Van Helmont thought the weight came from water alone. Scientists later found that much of it comes from carbon dioxide in the air. The process is called photosynthesis, a word for later grades.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (plants get materials for growth chiefly from air and water)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 5.1 Overview of Photosynthesis
Grokipedia, Jan Baptist van Helmont (the willow tree experiment)

blocks.html: At dinner, you might eat a root, a leaf and a flower without knowing it! Every vegetable and fruit comes from one part of a plant.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A potato is a stem that grows under the ground. Its "eyes" are buds.
Broccoli is a bunch of tiny flower buds.
It holds seeds, so it is a fruit.
Each kernel is a seed.

opts.readme: For each food, ask: which part of the plant is it?

blocks.cap: Which part of the plant do we eat?

blocks.html: We eat roots (carrots), stems (potatoes), leaves (lettuce), flowers (broccoli), fruits (apples, tomatoes) and seeds (peas, corn).
To find the part, ask how it grew. Did it grow down into the soil? Root. Is it thin and green? Leaf. Does it hold seeds? Fruit. Is it a bunch of tiny buds? Flower.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A potato grows under the ground. Is it a root?
steps: Look closely at a potato. It has little "eyes".
The eyes are buds. New shoots grow out of them.
Buds grow on stems, not on roots.
blocks.a: No. A potato is a stem that grows under the ground.

blocks.html: Many children say a potato is a root because it grows underground. It is a stem. And a celery stick is the stalk that holds up a celery leaf, so it is part of the leaf.

For the grown-up. Make a "plant parts" plate for a snack: a carrot stick, a piece of lettuce, a broccoli floret, an apple slice and a few peas. The Teddy Rook Book Food Garden Planner can help you grow some of them.
A puppy, a goldfish and a bird all look very different. But they need the same four things to stay alive.

blocks.name: bi-classify

bins: An animal does not need it

cards.why: Every animal needs oxygen from the air or from the water.
A safe place to rest and hide.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud, then sort it together.

blocks.cap: What does an animal need to live?

blocks.html: Animals need food, water, air and shelter, a safe place to rest and hide.
Food gives an animal energy to move and grow. Water keeps its body working. Air has oxygen, which every animal's body uses. Shelter keeps it safe from bad weather and from animals that might eat it.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A fish lives under water. Does it need oxygen?
steps: Every animal needs oxygen.
A little oxygen is mixed into the water.
A fish's gills take that oxygen out of the water as it flows past.
blocks.a: Yes. A fish gets its oxygen from the water with its gills.

blocks.name: bi-picture

items.label: fish: gills take oxygen from water
whale: comes up to breathe air

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Every animal needs oxygen. They get it in different ways.

blocks.html: Many children think only land animals need air. Fish need oxygen too; they take it from the water. Whales and dolphins swim up to the surface to breathe air, just like us.
For the grown-up. This builds on What Living Things Need. A goldfish bowl is a good example: the water needs to stay clean and have oxygen in it, which is why many fish tanks have a bubbler.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

blocks.html: What did you eat today? Maybe fruit, bread, cheese or chicken. Animals eat different things, too. Scientists sort them by what they eat.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A cow is big, but it eats grass.
A bear eats berries and nuts, and fish too.
A robin eats worms and berries.

opts.readme: Ask for each animal: what does it eat in the wild?

blocks.cap: Plant-eaters, meat-eaters, and animals that eat both.

blocks.html: Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat other animals. Omnivores eat both.
An animal's teeth or beak give a clue. Wide, flat teeth grind plants. Sharp, pointed teeth tear meat. Animals that eat both often have some of each kind.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A cow is huge and strong. Is it a meat-eater?
steps: What does a cow eat all day? Grass.
Grass is a plant.
Being big does not make an animal a meat-eater.
blocks.a: No. A cow is a plant-eater, an herbivore.

blocks.html: Children often think every big or scary-looking animal eats meat. Elephants, gorillas, cows and camels are big plant-eaters. And a bear, with its sharp claws, eats lots of berries and nuts as well as fish.
For the grown-up. People are omnivores too: we can eat plants and animals. Some families choose to eat no meat, and that is a choice people make, not a different kind of body.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

blocks.html: Look at a bird's beak. Is it long or short? Hooked or straight? The shape is a clue to what the bird eats. Every animal's body parts help it get food, move or stay safe.

blocks.name: bi-picture

items.label: hawk: hooked beak for tearing meat
hummingbird: long, thin beak for sipping nectar

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Each body part has a job.

blocks.html: Beaks, teeth, claws, feet, fins and shells each have a shape that fits a job.

A long, thin beak reaches deep into a flower, like a straw. A hooked beak tears meat. Webbed feet push water like paddles. Fins and a tail push a fish through the water. A turtle's hard shell keeps it safe.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A bird has a short, thick, strong beak. What does it most likely eat?
steps: A thick, strong beak can crack hard things, like a nutcracker.
Seeds have hard shells.
Many finches and sparrows have beaks like this.
blocks.a: Seeds.

blocks.html: Children often think all beaks or all teeth are the same. Look at the shape and ask what it could do: tear, grind, crack, sip or spear?

blocks.name: bi-classify

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. What is that body part for?

blocks.cap: What is each body part for?

blocks.html: For the grown-up. At a bird feeder or a park, look closely at beaks and feet. Ask: what could that shape be good for? Then watch the bird eat to see if you were right.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 1-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

blocks.html: Pet a dog and it feels soft. A bird feels fluffy. A snake feels smooth and dry. A frog feels cool and damp. An animal's covering is another clue to what kind of animal it is.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A snake has dry scales. It is not slimy.
A frog has smooth, moist skin.
A salamander has moist skin with no scales.

opts.readme: Ask: how would it feel if you could touch it?

blocks.cap: Fur, feathers, scales or moist skin?

blocks.html: Mammals have hair or fur. Birds have feathers. Fish and reptiles have scales. Amphibians have smooth, moist skin.

A covering protects an animal. Fur and feathers keep it warm. A reptile's dry scales keep its body from drying out in the sun. A frog's thin, moist skin even helps it breathe, but it dries out easily, so frogs stay near water.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Is a snake slimy?
steps: A snake is a reptile.
Reptiles are covered with dry scales.
A snake may look shiny, but it feels dry and smooth.
blocks.a: No. A snake has dry scales.

blocks.html: Many children think snakes are slimy. It is frogs, toads and salamanders, the amphibians, that have moist skin. Snakes and lizards are dry and scaly.
For the grown-up. At a nature center or a pet store, many children can gently touch a snake while a keeper holds it. The surprise that it feels dry makes the idea stick. Leave wild snakes alone.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (external structures)

blocks.html: Animals get around in many ways. They walk, run, hop, fly, swim, crawl and slither. Each body is shaped for the way it moves.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A penguin cannot fly. It swims with its wings.
A frog hops on land and swims in water.

opts.readme: Act out each one together: swim, fly, hop and slither!

blocks.cap: How does each animal move?

blocks.html: Legs walk, run and hop. Wings fly. Fins and tails swim. A snake bends its whole body to slither.

Strong back legs make a good hopper, like a rabbit or a frog. Light bones and wings make a good flyer. A smooth body with fins makes a good swimmer. No legs at all? A snake pushes its body against the ground.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A penguin has wings. Can it fly?
steps: A penguin's wings are stiff, flat flippers.
They are too small to lift it into the air.
Under water, it flaps them to zoom along.
blocks.a: No. A penguin uses its wings to swim.

blocks.html: Children often think anything with wings can fly, and every swimmer moves the same way. Penguins swim with their wings. A fish swishes its tail side to side, but a whale moves its tail up and down.

For the grown-up. Try the tail test at bath time or in a pool: wiggle your hand side to side like a fish tail, then up and down like a whale's. Whales and dolphins are mammals that breathe air, and their wide, flat tails beat up and down.
A kitten looks like a tiny cat. A puppy looks like a little dog. But a tadpole does not look like a frog at all! Young animals and their parents can look alike, or very different.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Some young look like their parents. Some change a lot.

blocks.html: Many young animals look like small copies of their parents. Others look very different and change as they grow. Many parents feed and protect their young.

Robin parents bring worms to their chicks all day. A mother duck leads her ducklings to food and watches for danger. Other young animals, like baby sea turtles, hatch and find their own way to the sea with no help.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Baby robins sit in the nest with their beaks open. How do their parents help them?
steps: The chicks cannot fly or find food yet.
The parents fly back and forth with worms and bugs.
They also keep the nest safe.
blocks.a: They bring them food and keep them safe.

blocks.html: Children often think every young animal is a small copy of its parents. A caterpillar, a tadpole and a fluffy chick look quite different from the grown-ups they become, but each grows into its own kind.

items: A young cat is a kitten. A young dog is a puppy.
A young cow is a calf. A young deer is a fawn.
A young bear is a cub. A young duck is a duckling.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Picture books of animal families are a good match for this topic. Ask, page by page: does the baby look like its parent? Who feeds it?

blocks.html: Dogs, mice, cows, bats, whales and you! What could all of these have in common? They are all mammals.
Mammals have hair or fur, breathe air with lungs, and feed their babies milk.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A whale breathes air and feeds its babies milk.
A bat has fur and feeds its babies milk, even though it flies.
A shark has gills: it is a fish.
An owl has feathers: it is a bird.

opts.readme: Ask for each one: does it have fur, and does it feed its babies milk?

blocks.cap: Mammal or not?

blocks.html: Where an animal lives does not decide its group. Its body does. A whale lives in the ocean, but it comes up to breathe air, and its babies drink milk. A bat flies, but it has fur and feeds its babies milk.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A dolphin swims in the sea. Is it a fish or a mammal?
steps: Does it breathe air? Yes, through a blowhole on top of its head.
Does it feed its babies milk? Yes.
Fish breathe with gills, and they do not make milk.
blocks.a: A dolphin is a mammal.

blocks.html: Children often call a whale or a dolphin a fish because it lives in water, and a bat a bird because it flies. Look for the mammal clues: hair, breathing air, and milk for the babies.
For the grown-up. People are mammals too. Ask your child to find the mammal clues on themselves: hair on their head, breathing air. It helps the idea feel real.
A robin, an owl, a duck, a penguin. Some fly high and some cannot fly at all. They are all birds. What makes a bird a bird?
Birds have feathers, a beak and two legs, and they hatch from eggs with hard shells. Only birds have feathers.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A penguin cannot fly, but it has feathers and a beak.
A bat flies, but it has fur. It is a mammal.
A butterfly flies, but it is an insect with six legs.

opts.readme: Ask for each one: does it have feathers?

blocks.cap: Bird or not?

blocks.html: Flying is not the test. Bats, bees and butterflies fly, and they are not birds. Penguins and ostriches cannot fly, but they are covered with feathers, so they are birds. Feathers are the clue that never fails.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A penguin cannot fly. Is it a bird?
steps: Does a penguin have feathers? Yes, thick waterproof ones.
Does it have a beak and two legs? Yes.
Only birds have feathers.
blocks.a: Yes. A penguin is a bird that swims instead of flying.

blocks.html: Many children think anything that flies is a bird, and that penguins and ostriches are not birds. Look for feathers. Bats and bees fly but have no feathers.
For the grown-up. If you see a feather on a walk, crouch down and look at it closely where it lies. Feathers come only from birds, so a feather means a bird was there.
Lots of animals live in water. But not all of them are fish! A fish has a special body for living under water its whole life.
Fish live in water, breathe with gills, swim with fins, and have a backbone. Most fish have scales.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A shark has gills and fins: it is a fish.
A whale breathes air: it is a mammal.
A jellyfish has no backbone, gills or fins.
A sea star is not a fish, even though people call it a starfish.
A crab has ten legs and a hard shell.

opts.readme: Ask for each one: does it have gills and fins?

blocks.cap: Fish or not?

blocks.html: Gills are the big clue. Water flows in through a fish's mouth and out past its gills, and the gills take oxygen from the water. A whale has no gills, so it must swim up to breathe air.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A jellyfish has "fish" in its name. Is it a fish?
steps: Does it have gills? No.
Does it have fins and a backbone? No.
A name can fool you. The body tells the truth.
blocks.a: No. A jellyfish is not a fish.

blocks.html: Children often call every water animal a fish: whales, dolphins, jellyfish, sea stars and crabs. Only animals with gills, fins and a backbone are fish. Sharks are fish!
For the grown-up. At an aquarium, play "fish or not?" at each tank. Look for gills (the slits or flaps behind the head) and fins.
Snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles look different. A turtle carries a shell, and a snake has no legs. But they belong to the same group: reptiles.
Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and breathe air with lungs. Most hatch from eggs laid on land.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A turtle has dry scales and breathes air all its life.
A frog has moist skin with no scales: it is an amphibian.
A salamander has moist skin: it is an amphibian.

opts.readme: Ask for each one: is its skin dry and scaly?

blocks.cap: Reptile or not?

blocks.html: Dry scales keep a reptile's body from drying out, so reptiles can live in hot, dry places like deserts. Even a sea turtle that swims all day has scaly skin and lungs. It swims up to breathe air.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A turtle lives in a pond. Is it a reptile or an amphibian?
steps: Its shell and skin are covered with dry scales.
It breathes air with lungs its whole life.
Amphibians have moist skin with no scales.
blocks.a: A turtle is a reptile.

blocks.html: Children often think turtles are amphibians because some live in water. Where it lives does not decide. Dry scales and lungs make a turtle a reptile.
For the grown-up. Many people are surprised that snakes feel dry. Reptiles also warm up by lying in the sun, which is why you see turtles stacked on logs on sunny days.
The word amphibian means "double life." Most amphibians start life in the water and live on land when they grow up. Frogs, toads and salamanders are amphibians.
Amphibians have smooth, moist skin with no scales. Most start life in water with gills and live on land as adults.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A salamander looks like a lizard, but its skin is moist with no scales.
A lizard has dry scales.
A tadpole is a young frog with gills.

opts.readme: Ask for each one: moist skin, or dry scales?

blocks.cap: Amphibian or reptile?

blocks.html: A frog's thin skin must stay damp, so amphibians live near water or in shady, wet places. A young frog, the tadpole, breathes with gills in the pond. As it grows, it starts breathing air.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A salamander has four legs and a long tail, like a lizard. Is it a lizard?
steps: Feel its skin (with your eyes!): it is smooth and moist.
It has no scales.
Lizards have dry scales. Moist skin means amphibian.
blocks.a: No. A salamander is an amphibian.

blocks.html: Children often think a salamander is a lizard because of its shape. Look at the skin. Moist and smooth: amphibian. Dry and scaly: reptile.
For the grown-up. Salamanders often hide under logs and rocks in damp woods. If you lift a log to look, do it gently, keep your hands off the animal, and put the log back the way it was.
Ants, bees, beetles, ladybugs and butterflies are insects. There are more kinds of insects than any other kind of animal! Here is how to tell if a small creature is one.
Insects have six legs and three body parts: a head, a middle and a back end. Many have wings.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A spider has eight legs and two body parts.
An earthworm has no legs at all.
A snail has a shell and no legs.

opts.readme: Count legs together: three on each side means an insect.

blocks.cap: Insect or not?

blocks.html: All six legs grow from the middle part of an insect's body. Count three on each side: 3 + 3 = 6. A spider has four on each side: 4 + 4 = 8. That is why a spider is not an insect.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Is a spider an insect?
steps: Count its legs: four on each side, so 8.
Count its body parts: 2.
Insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.
blocks.a: No. A spider is not an insect. It is an arachnid.

blocks.html: Children often call every small crawling animal a bug or an insect. Spiders have eight legs, and worms and snails have no legs at all, so none of them are insects.
For the grown-up. A magnifying glass makes leg-counting fun. Watch ants on a sidewalk or a beetle on a leaf, and count from a respectful distance.

sources.name: OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 15.3 Flatworms, Nematodes, and Arthropods

blocks.html: You know six animal groups now: mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects. Let's be animal detectives and sort them all, using body clues.

head: Group
Body clue
rows: hair or fur; milk for babies

blocks.html: To sort an animal, look for its body clue: fur, feathers, gills and fins, dry scales, moist skin, or six legs.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Breathes air and feeds its babies milk.
Feathers and a beak.
Fur, and milk for its babies.

opts.readme: Take turns: one person picks a card, the other names the body clue.

blocks.cap: Sort each animal into its group.

blocks.html: Where an animal lives and how it moves can fool you. Whales, sharks and penguins all swim. Bats, bees and robins all fly. Their bodies are different, and the body decides the group.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: This animal flies at night. It has fur and feeds its babies milk. What group is it in?
steps: Flying is not the clue.
Fur and milk are the mammal clues.
It is a bat.
blocks.a: Mammals.

blocks.html: Children often sort by home or movement: everything in water is a fish, everything that flies is a bird. Use the body clues instead.
For the grown-up. Play "twenty questions" with animals, but only allow body-clue questions: "Does it have feathers? Does it have six legs?"
Where do you live? You might say your house. But you also use your street, your yard, the park and the store. A wild animal uses a whole place like that, too. We call it a habitat.

blocks.name: bi-habitat

opts.readme: Name each animal. Ask: what does it eat here? Where does it hide?

blocks.cap: A pond is a habitat for many living things.

blocks.html: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives and finds the food, water and shelter it needs.
A frog needs bugs to eat, water to keep its skin moist, and mud or plants to hide in. A pond has all of that. So the pond, and the land around it, is the frog's habitat.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A robin builds a nest in a tree. Is the nest its habitat?
steps: The nest is where it keeps its eggs and chicks.
But it finds worms in the grass and water in puddles and streams.
All of those places together are its habitat.
blocks.a: No. The nest is its home. The whole forest or yard is its habitat.

blocks.html: Children often think a habitat is just a house, like a nest or a burrow. A habitat is the whole place, with everything the animal uses there.

blocks.name: bi-habitat

opts.readme: Your child taps the animals that live in a forest, then presses Check.

blocks.cap: Which of these live in a forest?

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Your backyard or a nearby park is a habitat. Make a list together of the living things you find there, and what each one might eat or hide in.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-ESS3-1: Earth and Human Activity (the relationship between the needs of animals and plants and the places they live)

blocks.html: Land habitats can be shady or sunny, wet or dry, warm or freezing. Here are four big ones: forests, grasslands, deserts and icy polar places.

blocks.name: bi-habitat

opts.readme: Talk about how hot and dry it is, and how these living things manage.

blocks.cap: A desert is full of life.

items: A forest has many trees growing close together.
A grassland is wide and open, covered with grass and few trees.
A polar place is cold and icy for much of the year.

blocks.html: Each land habitat has its own weather, so each has its own plants and animals.
What makes a desert a desert is dryness, not heat. Some deserts are hot in the day and cold at night. Some are cold all winter. Cactuses, lizards, snakes, hawks and kangaroo rats all live in deserts.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A kangaroo rat lives in the desert. How does it get water?
steps: There is very little water to drink in the desert.
A kangaroo rat eats seeds.
It gets the water it needs from its food.
blocks.a: From the seeds it eats. It almost never needs to drink.

blocks.html: Children often think deserts are always hot and have nothing living in them. Many deserts get cold, and all of them have plants and animals that are good at saving water.
For the grown-up. Polar bears live in the far north, near the North Pole. Most penguins live in the far south. They both live in icy places, but they never meet in the wild.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS4-1: Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (diversity of life in different habitats)

blocks.html: If you swim in the sea and get water in your mouth, it tastes salty. Pond water does not. That is the big difference between water habitats.

blocks.name: bi-habitat

opts.readme: Name each animal of the salty ocean.

blocks.cap: The ocean is salty.

items: Ponds and lakes hold fresh water that stays mostly still.
Rivers and streams hold fresh water that flows.

blocks.html: The ocean is salty water. Ponds, lakes and rivers are fresh water. Different animals live in each.
An animal's body is made for its own kind of water. Most ocean fish need salty water, and most pond fish need fresh water. If you moved them, most of them could not survive.

blocks.name: bi-habitat

opts.readme: Name each animal of the fresh-water pond.

blocks.cap: A pond holds fresh water.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Could a shark from the ocean live in a small pond?
steps: A shark is an ocean fish.
It needs salty water, and lots of room to swim.
A pond is small, and its water is fresh.
blocks.a: No. A shark needs the salty ocean.

blocks.html: Children often think all water is the same home, so an ocean fish could live in a pond. Salty water and fresh water are different habitats.
For the grown-up. Stir a spoonful of salt into one cup of water and leave another cup plain. Let your child taste a drop of each. That is the difference between ocean water and pond water.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 2-LS4-1: Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (diversity of life in different habitats)

blocks.html: A polar bear has a thick, warm coat. A camel has wide feet. A cactus has a fat, juicy stem. Each one has a body that is just right for where it lives.

blocks.name: bi-picture

items.label: thick fur and fat for the ice

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Made for their homes.

blocks.html: Living things have body parts that help them live in their own habitat.

A polar bear's thick fur and a layer of fat keep it warm on the ice. A camel's wide feet do not sink in sand, and it can go a long time without drinking. A cactus stores water in its thick stem, and its spines keep thirsty animals from eating it.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Could a polar bear live well in a hot desert?
steps: Its thick fur and fat are made to keep heat in.
In a hot desert it would get far too hot.
There would be no seals for it to hunt.
blocks.a: No. A polar bear is made for icy places.

blocks.html: Children often think an animal could live anywhere if it moved there. A polar bear would overheat in a desert, and a cactus would rot in a soggy swamp. Each is suited to its own home.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Thick feathers and fat keep it warm in icy water.
Long legs for wading.

opts.readme: Ask for each: what body part helps it live there?

blocks.cap: Which habitat is each one made for?

blocks.html: For the grown-up. A camel's hump stores fat, not water, which surprises many grown-ups too. The camel can use that fat when food is hard to find.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-LS4-3: Biological Evolution: Unity and Diversity (in a habitat, some organisms survive well, some less well)

blocks.html: Inside its habitat, an animal often has a special place to rest and stay safe. Some animals build their homes. Some dig them. Some find them.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A beaver builds a lodge of sticks and mud in the water.

opts.readme: Match each animal to its home.

blocks.cap: Who lives where?

blocks.html: Birds build nests, bees build hives, rabbits dig burrows, spiders spin webs, beavers build lodges, and bears rest in dens.
Each kind of animal makes the shelter that fits its life. A web catches a spider's food. A hive holds a bee family's honey. A lodge in the water keeps beavers safe from animals on land.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Does a deer live in a nest?
steps: A deer is too big for a nest.
It does not build a home at all.
It rests in thick bushes or tall grass, where it can hide.
blocks.a: No. A deer does not build a home.

blocks.html: Children often think every animal lives in a nest. Each kind of animal has its own kind of shelter, and some, like deer and many fish, have none at all.
For the grown-up. On a walk, look for animal homes: a nest in a bare tree in winter, a spider web on a fence, a hole at the base of a tree. Look, but leave them as they are.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-ESS3-1: Earth and Human Activity

blocks.html: People build roads, houses and gardens. That changes the land. But did you know animals and plants change the land too?

blocks.name: bi-picture

items.label: buries acorns that grow into trees
digs tunnels that let air into soil

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Living things change the places they live.

blocks.html: Plants, animals and people all change their surroundings as they meet their needs.

A beaver builds a dam to make deep water for its lodge, and a whole new pond forms. A squirrel buries acorns for winter and forgets some, so new oak trees grow. Tree roots grow thicker every year and push up sidewalks.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A beaver builds a dam across a stream. What happens?
steps: The dam holds back the water.
The water spreads out behind it.
A pond forms, a new home for frogs, ducks and fish.
blocks.a: A pond forms behind the dam.

blocks.html: Children often think only people change the land. Animals and plants change it too, a little at a time.
For the grown-up. Look for changes made by living things near you: a sidewalk lifted by roots, an anthill, a woodpecker's holes in a dead tree, or a path worn across the grass by people.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-ESS2-2: Earth's Systems (plants and animals can change their environment)

blocks.html: You need energy to run, jump and even think. Where does it come from? Your food! And where did the energy in your food come from? Follow it back far enough, and you always reach the sun.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb

opts.readme: Trace the arrows with a finger: sun, grass, rabbit, fox.

blocks.cap: Energy starts with the sun.

blocks.html: Plants use sunlight to make food. Animals get energy by eating plants, or by eating animals that ate plants.

Only plants (and a few tiny living things) can catch the sun's energy and store it in food. A rabbit eats grass and gets some of that energy. A fox eats the rabbit and gets some too. The energy passes along, from one living thing to the next.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A lizard lies on a warm rock in the sun. Is the sun giving it food energy?
steps: The sun warms the lizard, but warmth is not food.
The lizard gets its energy from the insects it eats.
The insects got theirs from plants, and the plants got it from the sun.
blocks.a: No. Its energy comes from its food, and that energy started with the sun.

blocks.html: Children often think the sun gives animals energy by warming them, or that animals make their own food like plants. Animal energy comes from food, and that energy came from the sun through plants.

For the grown-up. This connects Plants Make Their Own Food and Plant-Eaters, Meat-Eaters and Both. At a meal, pick one food and trace it back together: cheese came from milk, milk came from a cow, the cow ate grass, the grass used sunlight.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-PS3-1: Energy (energy in animals' food was once energy from the sun)

blocks.html: Grass grows in a meadow. A rabbit eats the grass. A fox eats the rabbit. That is a food chain: a list of who eats whom, with arrows.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb

opts.readme: Read the chain aloud: grass is eaten by the grasshopper, which is eaten by the mouse…

blocks.cap: Each arrow points from the food to the eater.

blocks.html: In a food chain, each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it. It shows where the energy goes.
Read an arrow as "is eaten by." Grass → rabbit means "grass is eaten by the rabbit." The energy in the grass goes into the rabbit, so the arrow points to the rabbit.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: An arrow goes from the mouse to the snake. What does it mean?
steps: Read the arrow as "is eaten by."
The mouse is eaten by the snake.
The mouse's energy goes into the snake.
blocks.a: The snake eats the mouse.

blocks.html: Many children draw the arrows backward, from the eater to the food, because they say "the fox eats the rabbit." Point the arrow the way the energy goes: from the rabbit into the fox.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb

opts.readme: Tap an animal. Green arrows show its food. Gold arrows show what eats it.

blocks.cap: Many chains join into a food web. Tap one to trace it.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Many food chains in one place join into a food web. When your child is older, the Science Lab's Predators and Prey simulation shows how the numbers in a web rise and fall.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS2-1: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers)
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 20.1 Energy Flow through Ecosystems

blocks.html: Every food chain starts the same way: with a plant. Scientists have special names for the plants that make food and the animals that eat.

blocks.name: bi-foodweb

opts.readme: Look at the colors. Green ones are producers. The others are consumers.

blocks.cap: A forest food web, colored by role.

blocks.html: Plants are producers: they make their own food. Animals are consumers: they eat to get their food.

To "produce" means to make. Plants make food from sunlight, air and water. To "consume" means to eat or use up. Animals cannot make food, so every animal is a consumer, from a tiny caterpillar to a big wolf.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: In the chain oak tree → caterpillar → robin → owl, which one is the producer?
steps: Which one makes its own food? The oak tree.
The caterpillar, the robin and the owl all eat.
The owl is at the end and is the strongest, but it still eats.
blocks.a: The oak tree.

blocks.html: Children sometimes call the big, strong animal at the end of a chain the producer. The producer is always the plant at the start, the one that makes food.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: A hawk eats, so it is a consumer.

opts.readme: Ask: does it make its own food, or does it eat?

blocks.cap: Producer or consumer?

blocks.html: For the grown-up. People are consumers too. A fun check at lunch: name one thing on the plate that came from a producer.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS2-1: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics
OpenStax, Concepts of Biology, 20.1 Energy Flow through Ecosystems

blocks.html: Every fall, trees drop millions of leaves. Logs fall. Plants and animals die. Why doesn't the forest fill up with dead things? Meet the clean-up crew: the decomposers.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: The clean-up crew.

blocks.html: Decomposers, like worms, mushrooms and tiny bacteria, break down dead plants and animals and put nutrients back into the soil.

Decomposers eat dead things bit by bit. As they do, the nutrients inside go back into the soil. New plants take those nutrients in through their roots. So nothing is wasted: it goes around and around.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A log lies in the forest for many years. What happens to it?
steps: Mushrooms and other fungi grow into the wood and soften it.
Insects, worms and bacteria eat it, little by little.
What is left becomes part of the soil.
blocks.a: Decomposers break it down into soil.

blocks.html: Children often think dead leaves and logs just disappear by themselves. Decomposers eat them, and that puts nutrients back into the soil for new plants.

For the grown-up. Turn over an old log in the woods (then put it back the way it was) and look for the crew: mushrooms, beetles, worms and soft, crumbly wood. A compost pile at home works the same way. This builds on Once Living.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 5-LS2-1: Ecosystems: Interactions, Energy, and Dynamics (decomposers)

blocks.html: A butterfly does not start life as a butterfly. It starts as a tiny egg on a leaf. Then it changes, and changes again, in one of the biggest makeovers in nature.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

notes: A butterfly lays a tiny egg on a leaf.
A caterpillar hatches. It eats leaves and grows and grows.
It hangs still and forms a chrysalis. Inside, its body changes.
A butterfly comes out, full size. It sips nectar from flowers.
opts.readme: Press Next together and read each note aloud.

blocks.cap: The life cycle of a butterfly, step by step.

blocks.html: Egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly. It is the same animal the whole time.

A caterpillar is an eating machine. It eats leaf after leaf and grows much bigger, shedding its skin as it goes. Then it stops, forms a chrysalis, and its body is rebuilt inside. When the butterfly comes out, it is done growing.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: You see a big butterfly and a small one. Is the small one a baby?
steps: A butterfly comes out of its chrysalis full size.
It does not grow after that.
All of its growing happened as a caterpillar.
blocks.a: No. The small one is a grown-up too, maybe of a smaller kind.

blocks.html: Children often think the caterpillar and the butterfly are two different animals, or that a butterfly keeps growing. It is one animal, and it does all its growing as a caterpillar.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Your child taps two pictures to swap them, then presses Check.

blocks.cap: Put the butterfly's life in order.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. In late summer, look for striped monarch caterpillars on milkweed plants. The whole change from egg to butterfly takes about a month in warm weather.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (life cycles)

blocks.html: In spring, look in a pond and you may see a clump of clear jelly with black dots. Those are frog eggs! Each dot can become a tadpole, and each tadpole can become a frog.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

notes: Eggs in jelly, in the water.
A tadpole hatches. It has a tail and gills, and lives in water.
Back legs grow, then front legs.
The tail shrinks. The young frog starts breathing air.
A grown frog, at home on land and in water.
opts.readme: Press Next together and read each note aloud.

blocks.cap: The life cycle of a frog, step by step.

blocks.html: Eggs → tadpole → tadpole with legs → froglet → frog.

A tadpole lives like a fish: it swims with its tail and breathes with gills. Little by little it changes. Legs grow, lungs grow, and its tail shrinks away until the young frog can hop out onto land and breathe air.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A tadpole swims and has gills. Is it a fish?
steps: A tadpole hatched from a frog's egg.
It will grow legs and lose its tail.
It can only grow into a frog, like its parents.
blocks.a: No. A tadpole is a young frog.

blocks.html: Children often think tadpoles are tiny fish. A tadpole is a young frog. It grows legs, its tail shrinks away, and it starts breathing air.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Your child taps two pictures to swap them, then presses Check.

blocks.cap: Put the frog's life in order.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. From egg to froglet takes weeks to months, depending on the kind of frog and how warm the water is. If you visit a pond in spring, look closely at the edges and leave the eggs and tadpoles where they are.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (life cycles)

blocks.html: Tap, tap, tap! Something is pecking inside the egg. Out comes a wet, wobbly chick. In a few hours it is dry and fluffy, and peeping for food.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Follow the arrows around the circle from the egg.

blocks.cap: The life cycle of a chicken.

blocks.html: Egg → chick hatching → chick → young chicken → grown hen or rooster.

A chick grows inside its egg for about three weeks while the egg is kept warm. It hatches covered in soft, fluffy down. Over the next several weeks its real feathers grow in, and it slowly looks more and more like its parents.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Is a chick born with long grown-up feathers?
steps: A new chick is covered in soft, fluffy down.
Real feathers grow in over several weeks.
By then it is a young chicken.
blocks.a: No. A chick hatches in soft down.

blocks.html: Children often think chicks hatch with grown-up feathers, or that a chick is a different kind of bird. A chick is a young chicken in fluffy down. It grows feathers as it grows up.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Your child taps two pictures to swap them, then presses Check.

blocks.cap: Put the chicken's life in order.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. A hen keeps her eggs warm by sitting on them; farms and schools sometimes use a warm box called an incubator. Chickens are a nice contrast to butterflies: a chick looks like a small, fluffy chicken from the start and simply grows.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 3-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (life cycles)

blocks.html: You have met four life cycles: a bean plant, a butterfly, a frog and a chicken. How are they the same? How are they different?

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.
Tadpole to frog.
A kitten looks like a small cat.
A chick looks like a small, fluffy chicken.
A ladybug starts as a larva that looks very different.

opts.readme: Ask: does the young one look like the grown-up?

blocks.cap: Changes shape, or just grows?

blocks.html: Every life cycle starts small, grows, and makes new young. Some young change shape completely; others look like small adults and just grow.

A butterfly has four very different stages. A frog changes slowly, from a swimming tadpole to a hopping frog. A chick and a kitten look like small versions of their parents from the start. A plant goes from seed to flower to seed again.

head: Life cycle
Stages
Big change?
rows: seed, sprout, young plant, flowers, pod

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Which changes shape completely as it grows: a butterfly or a kitten?
steps: A kitten looks like a small cat and just grows.
A caterpillar looks nothing like a butterfly.
It changes inside a chrysalis.
blocks.a: The butterfly.

blocks.html: Children often think every animal has the same number of stages. Count them for each one. A butterfly has four very different stages, while a chick just grows.
For the grown-up. Ask your child to draw two life cycles side by side, like a butterfly and a chicken, and circle the stage where each one does most of its growing.

blocks.html: Close your eyes. What can you hear? What can you smell? Your body has five ways to find out about the world. We call them the five senses.

blocks.name: bi-picture

opts.readme: Point to each part on your own face and hands as you read.

blocks.cap: The five senses and the body parts that use them.

blocks.html: We see with our eyes, hear with our ears, smell with our nose, taste with our tongue and feel with our skin.

Each sense sends messages to your brain. Your brain puts them together. When you eat, your tongue tastes sweet, salty, sour or bitter, and your nose smells the food at the same time. Together they make the flavor.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Your nose is stuffed up from a cold. Why does your food taste flat?
steps: When you chew, smells from the food rise up into your nose.
A stuffed nose blocks them.
Without the smells, food has much less flavor.
blocks.a: Your nose helps you taste, and it is blocked.

blocks.html: Many children think we taste only with the tongue. The nose does much of the work. That is why food tastes flat when a cold blocks your nose.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: You can smell them, and taste them too!

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Which sense would you use?

blocks.cap: Which sense do you use?

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Try the flavor test: hold your nose and eat a small piece of apple, then let go and take another bite. Many children are amazed at the difference.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-2: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (animals receive information through their senses)
National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH), Taste Disorders

blocks.html: A dog sniffs the ground and follows a smell you cannot even notice. An owl hunts in the dark. Many animals have senses much stronger than ours.

blocks.name: bi-picture

items.label: big eyes see in dim light

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Super senses.

blocks.html: Animals use their senses to find food and stay safe, and many can sense things we cannot.

An owl's huge eyes take in lots of light, so it can see when it is dim. A dog's nose has many more smell sensors than ours. Many bats call out and listen for the echoes that bounce back from insects. A cat's whiskers feel the air and nearby things.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: How can a bat find insects in total darkness?
steps: The bat makes high calls as it flies.
The sound bounces off an insect and comes back as an echo.
The bat hears the echo and knows where the insect is.
blocks.a: It uses its hearing and listens for echoes.

blocks.html: Children often think animals sense the world just as we do. A snake smells with its flicking tongue. A butterfly tastes with its feet. A dog smells things we never notice.

For the grown-up. Many bats use echoes, but not all. Some large fruit bats find food mostly by sight and smell. Play an echo game: in a big room or a tunnel, clap and listen for the sound to come back.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, 4-LS1-2: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

blocks.html: Scientists are great noticers. They look closely, listen, smell, touch and measure. What they notice is called an observation.
An observation is something you can see, hear, smell, feel or measure. A guess is what you think might be true.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: You cannot see a feeling.

cards.text: The leaf is as long as my hand.
The bird wants to go home.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud. Could a friend check it by looking, listening or measuring?

blocks.cap: Observation or guess?

blocks.html: Anyone can check an observation. If I say "the beetle has six legs," you can count them too. If I say "the beetle is sad," you cannot check that, because you cannot see a feeling. Scientists write down observations so others can check them.

items: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.
A ruler measures how long something is.
A thermometer measures how warm or cold something is.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: You watch an ant for one minute. Is "It carried a crumb three times" an observation?
steps: Did you see it? Yes.
Did you count it? Yes, three times.
A friend watching could check it too.
blocks.a: Yes, it is an observation.

blocks.html: Children often mix observations with guesses or feelings, like "the bug is sad." An observation is something you can see, hear, smell or measure, like "the bug has six legs."
For the grown-up. Start a nature notebook. Each day, draw one thing you saw outside and write one observation under it. The Teddy Rook Book Nature Study pages have ideas.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, Science and Engineering Practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations (grades K–2: make observations to collect data)

blocks.html: Look at the same tree in spring, summer, fall and winter. It looks like four different trees! But it is one tree, changing with the seasons.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Tap each season and talk about what the leaves are doing.

blocks.cap: One tree through the seasons. Tap a season.

blocks.html: Many trees grow new leaves in spring, are full and green in summer, change color and drop their leaves in fall, and rest bare in winter. Evergreens stay green all year.

In winter there is less light and the water in the ground may freeze. Leaves would not work well, so many trees drop them and rest. Before winter, the tree has already made tiny buds on its branches. In spring, the buds open into new leaves.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: A maple tree has no leaves in winter. Is it dead?
steps: Look closely at the tips of its twigs.
You can see small buds there.
The buds hold next spring's leaves.
blocks.a: No. The tree is resting.

blocks.html: Children often think trees die in winter because they are bare. They are resting. The buds for next spring's leaves are already on the branches.

blocks.name: bi-lifecycle

opts.readme: Follow the seasons around the circle.

blocks.cap: The seasons go around and around.

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Pick one tree near your home and take a photo of it once a month for a year. In winter, look closely at a twig together and find the buds.
Winter can be cold, snowy and short on food. Animals handle it in three main ways. Some leave, some sleep, and some keep going.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.why: Many geese fly south for the winter.
A groundhog sleeps deeply in its burrow all winter.
A deer stays active and eats twigs and buds.
A squirrel stays active and digs up nuts it buried.

opts.readme: Ask for each: does it fly away, sleep, or keep going?

blocks.cap: Migrate, hibernate, or stay active?

blocks.html: In winter some animals migrate to warmer places, some hibernate, and many stay active with thick fur and stored food.

To migrate is to travel to another place for the season, like geese flying south. To hibernate is to sleep very deeply, with a slow heartbeat and a cool body, living on stored fat. Groundhogs and some bats do this. Deer, foxes and squirrels stay awake and find what food they can.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Do all animals sleep through the winter?
steps: Geese and hummingbirds fly away.
Deer, foxes and squirrels stay active.
Only some, like groundhogs, sleep deeply all winter.
blocks.a: No. Most animals stay active or travel.

blocks.html: Children often think every animal sleeps all winter. Most stay active, many birds fly away, and only some, like groundhogs and some bats, truly hibernate.

For the grown-up. Bears are a famous puzzle: they sleep for months in winter, but their bodies do not cool down as much as a groundhog's, so scientists often call it a winter rest rather than true hibernation.
When the days get shorter and the air turns cool, animals get busy. They are getting ready for winter, long before the first snow.

blocks.name: bi-picture

items.label: gathers in flocks to fly south

opts.readme: Read the words aloud. Let your child tap and talk about each picture.

blocks.cap: Getting ready for winter.

blocks.html: In fall, animals store food, grow thicker coats, eat extra to build fat, or gather to fly south.

In winter, plants stop making seeds, nuts and berries, and many insects disappear. So animals get ready while food is still easy to find. Shorter days and cooler air are the signal that winter is coming.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: Why does a squirrel bury acorns in the fall?
steps: In fall, oak trees drop lots of acorns.
In winter, there will be none on the trees.
The squirrel saves some now and digs them up later.
blocks.a: So it has food in winter.

blocks.html: Children often think animals are surprised by winter. Many start getting ready in late summer and fall, when the days get shorter and food is still easy to find.

For the grown-up. In fall, watch a squirrel for a few minutes and count how many nuts it buries. Squirrels forget some of them, which is how many new oak trees get planted (see Living Things Change Their Surroundings).
A pet depends on you. It cannot fill its own water bowl or go to the store for food. Taking care of a pet is a big, kind job.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Cleaning the cage or litter box
cards.why: How often depends on the pet.

opts.readme: Read each card. How often does a pet need it?

blocks.cap: What does a pet need, and how often?

blocks.html: A pet needs food, fresh water, a clean home, exercise, gentle hands and visits to the vet.
A pet is an animal, and it has the same needs as every animal: food, water, air and shelter. In the wild it would find them itself. In our homes, we are the ones who give them, every single day.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: You are very busy today. Does your pet still need food and water?
steps: A pet needs food and water every day.
It cannot get them by itself.
Busy days count too.
blocks.a: Yes. Feed it and give it fresh water.

blocks.html: Children often think a pet needs care only when they feel like playing with it. A pet needs food and fresh water every day, even on busy days.
For the grown-up. A simple chart on the fridge, with a check box for food and water each day, helps a child own the job. A vet is the right person to ask what a particular pet needs.

sources.name: Next Generation Science Standards, K-LS1-1: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes (what animals need to survive)

blocks.html: A plant in a pot cannot reach out for rain or move to a sunny spot. If you have a plant at home, you are its helper.

blocks.name: bi-plant

opts.readme: Point to what the plant needs: light, water and air.

blocks.cap: A potted plant needs light, water and air.

blocks.html: A potted plant needs light, the right amount of water (not too much), a pot with holes for drainage, and room to grow.

Roots need air as well as water. Tiny spaces in the soil hold the air. If the soil stays soggy, water fills those spaces, and the roots can rot. Holes in the bottom of the pot let extra water drain out.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: When should you water most potted plants?
steps: Poke a finger into the soil.
If the top feels dry, it is time to water.
If it still feels wet, wait a day or two.
blocks.a: When the top of the soil feels dry.

blocks.html: Many children (and grown-ups!) think more water is always better. Too much water can drown the roots. Most potted plants like the soil to dry a little between waterings.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Water when the top of the soil is dry

cards.why: Too much water drowns the roots.

cards.text: Put it near a sunny window
Keep it in a dark closet
Use a pot with holes in the bottom

opts.readme: Read each card aloud and sort it together.

blocks.cap: Good plant care, or not?

blocks.html: For the grown-up. Different plants want different amounts of water: a cactus wants much less than a fern. The plant's tag or a garden center can tell you. This builds on What Plants Need.

University of Maryland Extension, Watering Indoor Plants

blocks.html: Parks, woods, ponds and beaches are habitats for many living things. When we visit, we are guests in their home.

blocks.name: bi-classify

cards.text: Watch animals quietly from far away
Put a rock back the way you found it
cards.why: The rock is a roof for the bugs under it.
Its parents are usually close by.

opts.readme: Read each card aloud and sort it together.

blocks.cap: Kind to nature, or not?

blocks.html: Watch wild animals without touching or chasing them, leave nests alone, put rocks back the way you found them, and keep trash out of nature.
A rock or a log can be a home for beetles, worms and salamanders, so we put it back. Chasing scares animals and wastes the energy they need. Trash can tangle or poison animals and plants.

blocks.title: Let's think it through
blocks.q: You find a young bird hopping on the ground. What should you do?
steps: Many young birds hop on the ground while they learn to fly.
Their parents are usually close by, watching and bringing food.
Taking it away would take it from its parents.
blocks.a: Leave it where it is, watch from far away, and tell a grown-up.

blocks.html: Children often think a young bird alone on the ground needs to be picked up and taken home, or that a rock is just a rock. The rock is someone's roof, and the bird's parents are often nearby. Tell a grown-up instead.

For the grown-up. Wildlife agencies such as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service say most young birds on the ground are fledglings being cared for by their parents, and the best thing to do is leave them alone. The Nature Study pages have more ways to explore outdoors.
